raw_row.Site_Description: The T2 (‘T’ for transportable) was developed in 1940 to replace Bellman Hangars. They were of a modular design meaning they could be dismantled, moved and reassembled elsewhere. Constructed of steel lattice portal frames and clad in galvanised corrugated iron. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF, and over 900 were built during the war. They were considered temporary structures with a limited design life, but many remain on airfields throughout the United Kingdom.
raw_row.condition_detail: This T2 is owned by Macrete, who manufacture concrete products within the hangar. It retains its original cladding but oddly is not in its original position. This is located on the line of the main runway. Therefore it must have been erected after the base closed. This would be consistent with the design of the T2 which was intended to be portable. Further evidence for the re-erecting of the hangar is the bases of the steel frames, which have been reinforced with concrete buttresses, suggesting the frames were cut at their base before removal for reassembly at the hangars’ current position. It is possible that this hangar is one of the two original sited on the northern end of the airfield. However, an aerial photograph from 1959 shows the two northern hangars removed with no hangar on this site.

raw_row.general_history: With the outbreak of war with Germany in 1914, the rapid expansion of the army led to a corresponding expansion of training facilities. By 1915 trench construction formed a major part of the training of recruits, reflection the prevailing methods of warfare on the Western Front.

raw_row.Site_Description: By 1942 the huge increase in aircraft numbers made the use of ‘frying pan’ dispersals unworkable. Consequently, the dispersals were redesigned into ‘spectacle’ dispersals sited around the perimeter track. They had many advantages over the earlier dispersals, notable they used less material for more parking. Aircraft could taxi onto one end then follow a shallow curve back onto the perimeter track. This reduced the fatigue on air-frames and allowed squadrons to be rapidly deployed.

raw_row.Site_Description: During the inter-war period, there was no provision or need for aircraft dispersal at UK airfield. However, in February 1939 orders were issued for the dispersal of aircraft within the perimeter. Initially, short trackways were used but they were upgraded with ‘Frying Pan’ dispersals sited along the perimeter track. The dispersal was normally 125-150 feet wide (though often smaller on fighter airfields), but drawbacks were soon revealed. One aircraft leaving its dispersal would clog up the access track, causing congestion as aircraft numbers increased during the war. Furthermore, as aircraft taxied off the pan they needed to perform a tight 180 degrees turn for which aircraft undercarriages and tyres were not designed.

raw_row.Site_Description:
The magazine is a prefabricated design produced by the Armco International Corporation of Middletown Ohio, and sometimes referred to as Armco huts. Measuring 20' x 50', the structure is a curved steel hut with steel end walls, covered with a layer of earth to provide extra protection, which was then seeded to provide a level of camouflage. Ventilation was provided in the headwall to prevent condensation within the magazine. The magazines at Fincarn were used to store five and three inch naval shells, torpedo warheads, depth charges and small arms ammunition. These were brought to the US navy operating base at Lisahally.

Stencilling remains on the outer face of the head wall. A number  (circa eight though there could be more) of contemporary doodles remain to the left and right of the doorway and on the rear wall, which include images of Mickey Mouse, Churchill (possibly), Hitler and unidentified women.
raw_row.condition_detail: Site is heavily overgrown but largely intact, although one of the doors has fallen off its hinges. A section of the steel head wall is bulging out from the face due to pressure from the soil overburden.

raw_row.general_history: The Nissen hut was invented in 1915 by Canadian Col. P. N. Nissen. Prefabricated and designed to be erected quickly, in WW2 the Nissen hut became one of the standard forms of temporary building for all types of accommodation. The 16 foot span hut was semi-circular in section and could be built to any length in multiples of 6 foot bays, normally 6. The frame of steel ribs was covered with corrugated steel sheets held in place by the ribs and straining wires. The end walls could be timber or brick, containing 2 windows and a door. Type A huts were for officers and consisted of 4 rooms and one for servants. Type B huts were for sergeants and were a single room accommodating 8 men. Those for other ranks or airmen accommodated 12 men in a single room. A 24 and 30 foot span design were constructed in the same way but had dormer windows and door cheeks fitted along the sides.

raw_row.general_history: The location of Northern Ireland on the western edge of the United Kingdom suggested that the region may be insulated from the threat of German bombing raids. Plans laid down by the government in London for the defence of Britain and Northern Ireland assumed that air defences in England would protect the province. After the Munich crisis of 1938, A re-evaluation of air defences recommended that Belfast be protected by a single fighter squadron, twenty-four heavy (HAA), and twenty-four light anti-aircraft (LAA) guns. Nevertheless, with the advent of war, Belfast was considered an unlikely target for German raids. Consequently, few guns were committed to the defence of the city and none were supplied to protect the rest of the north. The fall of France in June 1940 brought Northern Ireland well within the range of air attacks from German bases in northern France. Therefore recommendations were made to double the strength of the gun defences in the province, but shortages of equipment meant that on the eve of the air raids on Belfast in the spring of 1941, Belfast was defended by sixteen HAA guns (in four batteries), and six LAA guns. The damage and human toll inflicted by the Luftwaffe raids on the nights of 15 April and 4-5 May was devastating, with over 1,000 people killed and almost half the housing stock of the city rendered uninhabitable. Shocked into action by the appalling loss of life and damage to industry, the anti-aircraft defences were significantly reinforced. Four Gun Defended Areas (GDA) were established; Belfast, Larne, L’Derry and Lough Erne. Twelve HAA batteries surrounded the periphery of Belfast, while seven HAA batteries were built around L’Derry and the Foyle estuary, and two each at Larne and Lough Erne.
raw_row.Site_Description: HAA batteries were typically armed with four 3.7-inch heavy anti-aircraft guns, which could fire a 28-pound projectile to an effective ceiling of 32,000 feet. The gun crews were directed from the battery command post. The command post provided height, direction and altitude data to the gun pits to enable the gun layers to set the fused to detonate at the correct altitude. Most batteries had a ramp and platform nearby which held the gun laying (GL) radar. A polygonal mat surrounded the GL radar, marking the area of the false datum, which was composed of a wire mesh and was needed to generate a false horizon for the primitive GL radar sets.

raw_row.general_history: The Romney hut (also known as a shed) was designed in Romney House, London by the Directorate of Fortifications and Works at the start of WW2. Primarily used for storage, they could be adapted for canteens, workshops and even cinemas. Semi-circular in section, the hut was a series of tubular steel ribs curved to a radius of 17 feet 6 inches. The were bolted to the foot and connected by steel purlins. The frame was covered by corrugated iron sheeting. The inside of the structure was normally unlined. The hut was composed of any number of bays each 8 feet wide (usually 96 feet long) and an internal span of 35 feet.
raw_row.Site_Description: Romney pre-fabricated hut, likely used as a store.
raw_row.condition_detail: Site appears intact and in good condition

raw_row.Site_Description: The small brick and concrete shelter protected the crew tasked with operating the decoy site during a raid. raw_row.general_history: The Nissen hut was invented in 1915 by Canadian Col. P. N. Nissen. Prefabricated and designed to be erected quickly, in WW2 the Nissen hut became one of the standard forms of temporary building for all types of accommodation. The 16 foot span hut was semi-circular in section and could be built to any length in multiples of 6 foot bays, normally 6. The frame of steel ribs was covered with corrugated steel sheets held in place by the ribs and straining wires. The end walls could be timber or brick, containing 2 windows and a door. Type A huts were for officers and consisted of 4 rooms and one for servants. Type B huts were for sergeants and were a single room accommodating 8 men. Those for other ranks or airmen accommodated 12 men in a single room. A 24 and 30 foot span design were constructed in the same way but had dormer windows and door cheeks fitted along the sides.

raw_row.Site_Description: Building first indicated on the 1904 Ordnance Survey Map and from its detail clearly built at the same time as the adjacent buildings along the boundary wall (numbers 62 and 59 HB01/09/002 N&Q) and designed by the same person. The date of this wall may be from the 1870’s for the main post 1891 expansion is surrounded by a much lower brick wall and fence but there is no documentary evidence to support this. Original function of building has not been ascertained though from evidence of a late 19th century photograph it appears that it may have been stables. A picket fence presumably to contain animals is erected in front in the photographs. Building subsequently converted to storage.
raw_row.condition_detail: Site is intact and in good condition.
raw_row.Other_Sources: HB file for HB01/09/002 R

raw_row.Site_Description: A ‘Tannoy’ system was used to communicate instructions to personnel across the airfield via loudspeakers across the airfield. These were connected to the amplifying equipment which was found in the Speech Broadcasting Building.
